title: Foundations and how to read a call
summary: What SIP is for, which network facts it assumes, and how to read a ladder without inventing rules.

lessons.title: What SIP is for
lessons.summary: SIP creates, changes, and ends sessions, while RTP carries the media those sessions describe.
objectives: Separate SIP signaling from RTP media
Name user agent, proxy, registrar, and redirect server
Treat 100 Trying as hop-by-hop quench, not as an answer

illustration.title: Two planes
illustration.caption: SIP agrees the session. SDP names the media. RTP moves the samples.

layers.name: SIP
layers.detail: INVITE, responses, dialogs, teardown

layers.name: SDP
layers.detail: Offer and answer: address, port, codec

layers.name: RTP
layers.detail: Packetized media after the answer

paragraphs: SIP is an application-layer protocol for creating, modifying, and terminating sessions among one or more participants. A phone call is the usual session, and the protocol still does not define the audio coding or the packet format of the voice.

RTP carries the media packets. SDP, carried inside SIP, is the offer and the answer that name the addresses, ports, and codecs. Read RFC 3261 for the signaling rules and keep the media RFCs beside it.

A user agent originates or answers a request. A proxy routes requests and responses. A registrar accepts REGISTER and stores the Contact bindings for an address-of-record. A redirect server answers with a 3xx and leaves the path.

An SBC is usually a back-to-back user agent: it terminates one dialog and creates another. RFC 7092 is the taxonomy, and RFC 5853 collects the deployment requirements. Naming the role in a trace is the useful step. The product logo is not a protocol role.

lessons.title: Ports, transports, and where a request can go
lessons.summary: SIP uses UDP or TCP on 5060 and TLS on 5061, and a request that does not fit one datagram needs a connection.
objectives: State the default ports for UDP, TCP, and TLS
Explain why a large INVITE moves off UDP
Recognize WebSocket as a transport, not a new method set

illustration.title: Defaults operators meet
illustration.caption: A peer document can override a default. The default is the rule when the peer is silent.
rows: Same methods, WS or WSS in Via

paragraphs: RFC 3261 section 18 sets UDP and TCP on port 5060 and TLS on port 5061. UDP is why INVITE retransmissions exist: the transaction layer repeats a request that may have been lost.

A request that does not fit in one datagram belongs on a connection-oriented transport. TCP and TLS use Content-Length to find the end of the message. WebSocket, RFC 7118, carries the same SIP messages with transport tokens WS and WSS.
A sips URI asks for TLS on the signaling hop. The method names, the dialog rules, and the SDP offer do not change because the Via says TLS.
When a deployment encrypts the media, that keying is negotiated in SDP, for example with DTLS-SRTP. Read the Via transport, the sent-by host, and the port before you argue about certificates.

lessons.title: E.164, sip URIs, and tel URIs
lessons.summary: A global number is written in a tel URI or in a sip URI user part, and E.164 is the numbering plan those digits follow.
objectives: Read a global tel URI and a sip URI with user=phone
Say what E.164 is without inventing an ITU clause
Keep the Request-URI and the To URI as different fields

illustration.title: Three ways the same number appears
illustration.caption: The digits are the numbering plan. The scheme decides who can route the identifier.
rows: A number plus a SIP domain

sections.h: The number and the URI are different layers
paragraphs: RFC 3966 defines the tel URI. A global number begins with +. The user part of sip:+15551212@example.com is that same kind of number when the URI carries user=phone.

E.164 is the ITU-T numbering plan those digits follow. This course cites RFC 3966 for the URI syntax and does not invent an ITU clause number. When a ticket says E.164, check the digits and the leading +, then check which URI scheme is on the wire.

sections.h: A tel URI has no domain to look up
paragraphs: A tel URI does not name a host, so a SIP element that must forward it builds a sip URI. The telephone-subscriber goes in the user part, and the host becomes the domain that should route it.

The Request-URI is where this hop sends the request. The To header is the logical destination the caller identified. They often look alike on the first INVITE and they diverge as soon as a proxy retargets.

lessons.title: How to read an RFC
lessons.summary: A SIP argument cites the RFC number and the section, and the normative sentences outrank a broken example.
objectives: Separate Standards Track text from an Informational map
Cite a rule by RFC and section
Use the ABNF and the prose together

illustration.title: Where to open RFC 3261
illustration.caption: Memorize the chapter map. You will use it every time a trace disagrees with a product screen.
rows: A tag or a branch is in question

paragraphs: The top of an RFC tells you the status. RFC 3261 is Standards Track. An Informational RFC can index the others and it does not replace a Standards Track rule.

MUST, SHOULD, and MAY are the requirement words. A SHOULD is a rule you depart from only with a reason you can write down. When an example and a normative sentence disagree, follow the sentence and the ABNF in section 25.
Section 20 is the header catalog. Section 21 is the response codes. Section 7 is how a message is formed, including compact names. Quoting a vendor slide is not a citation.
Do not paste the RFC into a runbook. Paraphrase the rule and link to the RFC editor. The legal terms for the text itself are covered in the licensing lesson.

sections.h: An index is not the protocol
paragraphs: RFC 5411 is Informational. It lists the SIP specifications so you can find the document that owned a behavior when the guide was published. It is not a substitute for RFC 3261.

When a header is absent from section 20 of RFC 3261, look for an extension. PRACK is RFC 3262. UPDATE is RFC 3311. Session timers are RFC 4028. REFER is RFC 3515. The guide helps you discover that split.

sections.h: The map stopped. The protocol did not
paragraphs: A snapshot cannot include documents published after it. RFC 6026 corrects INVITE 2xx handling. RFC 6141 tightens target refresh. RFC 6665 is the events specification. RFC 7118 adds WebSocket.

Use 5411 to choose a starting document, then read that document and anything that updates it. If a header is only in the guide's table and not in the extension you implemented, you do not have the rule yet.

sections.h: The protocol text has a license
paragraphs: SIP is specified by the IETF. The terms for using that text are the IETF Trust Legal Provisions. Read them before you copy specification text into a product, a course pack, or a customer document.

This course paraphrases rules and links the RFCs. It is not legal advice, and it does not tell you that a particular copy is permitted. If you need a permission, read the trust provisions or ask counsel.

sections.h: Codecs are not the SIP license
paragraphs: Opus is specified in RFC 6716. The license the codec project publishes is at the Opus license page, and patent disclosures are listed in the IETF IPR disclosure system. Read those three. This lesson does not clear a product.
G.711 and G.729 are ITU-T recommendations. Cite those recommendations for the codec. Patent status for G.729 has to be verified against current sources. This course states no expiry date.

sections.h: The start line and the routing budget
paragraphs: A request starts with the method, the Request-URI, and SIP/2.0. The first Via names the transport and the address where this hop wants the response, and the branch parameter identifies the transaction.

A branch written by an implementation of this specification begins with the magic cookie z9hG4bK. The UAC inserts Max-Forwards, and the initial value SHOULD be 70. Each proxy that forwards the request decrements it by one.

The From header on a request the UAC creates carries a tag. The To header on a request outside a dialog has no tag. Call-ID is the third piece of dialog identity, together with those two tags once the To tag exists.

CSeq is a number plus the method token. Contact on an INVITE is the remote target the answerer will use later. The addresses 203.0.113.10, 203.0.113.20, 198.51.100.30, and 192.0.2.40 are documentation ranges from RFC 5737, not production hosts.

sections.h: The same box changes roles per request
paragraphs: The UAC is the role that creates a request. The UAS is the role that creates the response. A phone is a UAC for the INVITE it sends and a UAS for the INVITE it answers.

A stateful proxy maintains the transaction, adds a Via with its own branch, and decrements Max-Forwards. A stateless proxy forwards without that transaction state and does not generate its own 100 Trying. A redirect server returns 3xx with a Contact and does not stay in the dialog.

The registrar accepts REGISTER and writes bindings into a location service. The proxy reads that location service when it retargets. RFC 3261 keeps those roles separate even when one product runs both.

A B2BUA is a UAS glued to a UAC. It usually creates a new Call-ID on the outgoing side. RFC 7092 classifies that behavior, and RFC 5853 describes SBC requirements. If the Call-ID changes in the middle of the ladder, you are not looking at a pure proxy.

lessons.summary: The core methods are INVITE, ACK, OPTIONS, BYE, CANCEL, and REGISTER, and status codes fall into six classes.

paragraphs: RFC 3261 defines INVITE, ACK, OPTIONS, BYE, CANCEL, and REGISTER. INVITE sets up a session. ACK finishes the INVITE handshake. BYE ends a confirmed dialog. CANCEL asks to abandon an INVITE that has no final response yet.
OPTIONS asks for capabilities and does not set up a session. REGISTER writes bindings. PRACK, UPDATE, and REFER are extension methods: RFC 3262, RFC 3311, and RFC 3515. They do not replace the six.
100 Trying is hop by hop. 180 means ringing. 183 means session progress and often carries early media SDP. 200 OK is success. 302 moves you to a Contact.

401 Unauthorized challenges a UAS or registrar with WWW-Authenticate. 407 Proxy Authentication Required challenges a proxy. 486 is Busy Here. 487 is Request Terminated, the usual final response after a successful CANCEL. 603 Decline is a global rejection. Section 22 is the authentication chapter.

lessons.title: Headers and compact forms
lessons.summary: Compact header names are aliases from RFC 3261, with a few more aliases defined in the extension RFCs.
objectives: Expand the RFC 3261 compact forms
Keep extension compact forms with their RFCs
See why rewriting From or To breaks dialog matching

illustration.title: Compact names
illustration.caption: One character is the whole header name. Unknown one-letter names are not a license to invent aliases.

sections.h: Long form and short form are one header
paragraphs: A header is a name, a colon, and a value. RFC 3261 defines compact forms for ten headers: c Content-Type, e Content-Encoding, f From, i Call-ID, k Supported, l Content-Length, m Contact, s Subject, t To, and v Via.

The compact form is only a size alias. f is From, including the tag. A parser that stores the long name and a parser that stores the short name are talking about the same field. Section 7.3.3 and section 20 are the citations.
Event's compact form is o, and Allow-Events is u. Those two come from RFC 6665, not from the base list. Refer-To is r and Referred-By is b, from RFC 3515.

Rewriting From, To, or Call-ID is not a compact-form conversion. Those fields are the dialog identity. A SIP profile that substitutes a different URI into From will make the peer's later requests fail to match the dialog.

lessons.title: Transactions and the branch cookie
lessons.summary: A transaction is identified by the branch, and a retransmission repeats that branch instead of starting a new one.
objectives: Use the branch as the transaction id
Separate a retransmission from a new request
Apply the ACK branch rule for 2xx and non-2xx

illustration.title: INVITE client transaction
illustration.caption: Calling retransmits. Proceeding waits. A 2xx is handed to the transaction user because its ACK is a new transaction.

paragraphs: The branch parameter identifies the transaction. An implementation of RFC 3261 starts it with z9hG4bK and makes the rest unique across space and time. A retransmission sends the same request again, including that branch.

CANCEL is an exception: it uses the same branch as the INVITE it cancels. The ACK for a non-2xx final response uses that same branch too. The ACK for a 2xx does not. It is a different transaction, so it gets a new branch.

sections.h: INVITE is the special state machine
paragraphs: On UDP the client starts in Calling, retransmits at T1 doubling, and starts Timer B at 64 times T1. A provisional response moves it to Proceeding and stops those retransmissions. If Timer B fires, the client must not invent an ACK.

The overview in section 17 calls INVITE a three-way handshake. RFC 6026 corrects the 2xx path: the transaction user sends the end-to-end ACK, and the transaction layer absorbs late 2xx responses. The non-2xx ACK is still generated hop by hop inside the INVITE transaction.

lessons.title: Dialog identity
lessons.summary: A dialog is identified by Call-ID, the From tag, and the To tag, and the initial request has no To tag.
objectives: Name the three dialog-id components
Tell an early dialog from a confirmed dialog
Increment CSeq for a new request inside the dialog

illustration.title: Dialog states
illustration.caption: No dialog exists until a response carries a To tag. BYE moves a confirmed dialog to terminated.

paragraphs: Dialog identity is the Call-ID, the From tag, and the To tag. At the UAC the local tag is the From tag and the remote tag is the To tag. At the UAS the local and remote tags are swapped, and the three values are the same set.

A request outside a dialog has no To tag. The UAS puts the tag on the response that creates the dialog. A 100 Trying SHOULD NOT add that tag. A 180 or 183 that includes a tag creates an early dialog. A 2xx to the INVITE confirms it.

The remote target is the Contact URI from the other side. Later requests in the dialog use that URI as the Request-URI, and they carry both tags. The route set, if Record-Route was present, is stored with the dialog.

The CSeq number increases for each new request the UAC sends inside the dialog. ACK and CANCEL are the exceptions that keep the INVITE's number and change only the method token. BYE is a new request, so its CSeq number is higher, and it is how a confirmed dialog ends.

lessons.title: T1, the transaction timeout, and Timer C
lessons.summary: T1 seeds retransmissions, 64 times T1 ends the transaction, and Timer C is the proxy's longer INVITE arm.
objectives: State the defaults for T1, T2, and T4
Compute Timer B as 64 times T1
Keep Timer C separate from Timer B

illustration.title: Clocks from the timer table
illustration.caption: Change T1 and every timer that scales with it changes. Timer C does not use that formula.
rows: Timer B and Timer F give-up
Proxy wait for a final INVITE response
Retransmit cap, and time left in the network

paragraphs: T1 is an estimate of the round trip and defaults to 500 ms. On UDP, Timer A starts at T1 and doubles after each INVITE retransmission while the client is in Calling. A reliable transport does not start Timer A.

T2 defaults to 4 seconds and caps the spacing of non-INVITE retransmissions and of INVITE response retransmissions. T4 defaults to 5 seconds and is the time a message may still be in the network. Timer I and Timer K use T4 on UDP so a stray retransmission can be absorbed.

Timer B is the INVITE transaction timeout and Timer F is the non-INVITE transaction timeout. Both are 64 times T1, which is 32 seconds at the default. Seven UDP transmissions fit in that window. If Timer B fires, the client does not generate an ACK.

Timer C belongs to the proxy, not to that formula. It is how long a proxy will wait for a final response to INVITE, and the table sets it at more than 3 minutes. A proxy that abandons an INVITE at 32 seconds is applying Timer B's number to Timer C's job.

lessons.title: Two different ACK rules
lessons.summary: The ACK for a non-2xx is hop by hop inside the INVITE transaction, and the ACK for a 2xx is a new end-to-end transaction.
objectives: Reuse the INVITE branch only for a non-2xx ACK

illustration.title: Which ACK is this?
illustration.caption: Look at the status code first, then the branch.
rows: UAC transaction user, end to end
ACK is still end to end

paragraphs: A final response from 300 through 699 is acknowledged by the INVITE client transaction. That ACK uses the INVITE's branch, the INVITE's CSeq number, and the method token ACK. Each hop generates its own ACK. A proxy does not forward the caller's ACK downstream.

The ladder below is that case. The proxy ACKs the peer with branch z9hG4bKproxy01, the same branch it put on the forwarded INVITE. The caller ACKs the proxy with branch z9hG4bKalice01. Neither ACK is a new transaction.

The ACK for a 200 OK is sent by the UAC using the dialog route set and the remote target. It carries a new branch because it is a different transaction. The CSeq number still matches the INVITE. Proxies that record-routed forward this ACK as they would any other mid-dialog request.

RFC 3261's overview describes INVITE as a three-way handshake, and that sentence is too small for the 2xx case. RFC 6026 corrects the state machine so a late 2xx is absorbed by the transaction, while the ACK remains the UAC's end-to-end request. The UAS retransmits the 200 OK until that ACK arrives.

paragraphs: A proxy that wants later dialog requests inserts a Record-Route before any Record-Route already on the request. The URI is a sip or sips URI and it MUST contain lr. The UAS copies those values into the response in the same order.

The UAS route set is the request's Record-Route list in that order, so the proxy beside the UAS is first. The UAC route set is the response's Record-Route list in reverse order, so the proxy beside the UAC is first. The remote target is the Contact, and that becomes the Request-URI of the ACK.

With lr, each hop removes a top Route that names itself and forwards toward the next Route, leaving the Request-URI as the remote target. A missing lr falls into the older strict-routing procedure, which rewrites the Request-URI.

On this ladder the peer sees Core and then Edge. The caller reverses that into Edge and then Core. The ACK's first Route is 203.0.113.20. Edge will pop that Route and forward the ACK toward 198.51.100.30.

lessons.title: PRACK and reliable provisionals
lessons.summary: A provisional response with Require: 100rel is retransmitted until PRACK, and RAck names that exact response.
objectives: Offer 100rel and answer with RSeq
Build RAck from RSeq and the INVITE CSeq
Give PRACK its own CSeq number

illustration.title: RAck fields
illustration.caption: The first number is the provisional. The next two name the INVITE, not the PRACK.

paragraphs: RFC 3262 adds the option tag 100rel. The UAC puts it in Supported, or in Require when it will not proceed without reliable provisionals. The UAS sends the provisional with Require: 100rel and an RSeq number.

Until PRACK arrives, the UAS retransmits that provisional. 100 Trying is not made reliable this way. The responses you will see with RSeq are 180 and 183. Early media SDP in a 183 is reliable only after the PRACK succeeds.

PRACK uses a new branch and the next CSeq number in the dialog. RAck carries three tokens: the RSeq, the CSeq number of the request being acknowledged, and that request's method. For the first INVITE that is RAck: 1 1 INVITE when RSeq is 1.

The UAS answers PRACK with 200 OK and CSeq 2 PRACK. That 200 is not the INVITE's final response. The INVITE transaction is still open until its own final response, and the ACK rules for that final response are unchanged.

lessons.title: UPDATE before the INVITE completes
lessons.summary: UPDATE can change the session while the initial INVITE is still outstanding, and it does not use the ACK rules.
objectives: Send UPDATE only when no offer is outstanding
Treat UPDATE as a non-INVITE transaction
Keep dialog identifiers stable across the session change

illustration.title: Offer, answer, then a new offer
illustration.caption: The INVITE offer is answered in the 183. UPDATE is the next offer. The INVITE is still open.

paragraphs: RFC 3311 defines UPDATE. It can be sent in an early dialog, before the initial INVITE transaction completes, and it can be sent again after the dialog is confirmed. Success is 200 OK. There is no ACK for UPDATE.
UPDATE uses the next CSeq number and a new branch. Call-ID and both tags stay the same. That is the dialog. Changing the session description does not mint a new dialog id.

If the INVITE carried an offer, wait until that answer has been sent and, when 100rel is in use, acknowledged, before UPDATE carries another offer. Two offers outstanding at once is not a legal offer/answer exchange.

An SDP-only UPDATE changes the session. It is not the target-refresh procedure. Changing the remote target URI is covered by RFC 6141, and the mid-dialog request that operators use for that change is the re-INVITE. Read 6141 before you treat a new Contact as harmless.

lessons.title: Session-Expires and 422
lessons.summary: Session timers name who refreshes the dialog, and 422 tells the caller the interval was below Min-SE.
objectives: Read Session-Expires and the refresher parameter
Retry after 422 using the Min-SE from the response
Refresh with re-INVITE or UPDATE before the interval ends

illustration.title: Timer headers
illustration.caption: Min-SE is a floor. The absolute minimum in the specification is 90 seconds.
rows: Lowest interval this UA will accept
Ask again with a higher floor

paragraphs: RFC 4028 adds Session-Expires and Min-SE. The interval is in seconds. The refresher parameter is uac or uas and names who will send the refresh. Supported: timer means the UA can do this. Require: timer means the other side must.

Min-SE MUST NOT be lower than 90 seconds. A request may still be too small for the peer. The peer then answers 422 Session Interval Too Small and includes the Min-SE it will accept. That 422 is a non-2xx final response, so it is acknowledged inside the INVITE transaction.

The UAC retries with Session-Expires at least as large as the received Min-SE, and it raises its own Min-SE to that value. If the UAC asked to be the refresher and the UAS agrees, the 200 OK repeats refresher=uac.

The refresher sends a re-INVITE or an UPDATE before the interval expires. If the refresh does not happen, the UA treats the session as finished and sends BYE. The refresh is ordinary dialog work. It does not create a new Call-ID.

lessons.title: CANCEL, BYE, and re-INVITE
lessons.summary: CANCEL abandons an unanswered INVITE, BYE ends a confirmed dialog, and re-INVITE changes a dialog that already exists.
objectives: Pair 200 OK for CANCEL with 487 for the INVITE
Use BYE only on a confirmed dialog
Treat a mid-dialog INVITE as a re-INVITE and a possible target refresh

illustration.title: Three requests people mix up
illustration.caption: The dialog state decides the method. The branch decides whether CANCEL matches.
rows: 200 for CANCEL, 487 for INVITE, then ACK
The other INVITE is still open

paragraphs: CANCEL uses the same Request-URI, Call-ID, From, To, and CSeq number as the INVITE, and the same branch. The method token is CANCEL. It applies only while that INVITE has no final response. The UAS answers 200 OK to the CANCEL.

If the UAS stops the INVITE, the INVITE's final response is 487 Request Terminated. That 487 is a non-2xx, so the ACK reuses the INVITE branch. A 200 OK to CANCEL means the CANCEL was received. It does not mean the INVITE is already dead.

sections.h: BYE and re-INVITE need the dialog
paragraphs: BYE is sent only in a confirmed dialog, with both tags and a higher CSeq. If a 200 OK to the INVITE crosses the CANCEL, the dialog is confirmed and CANCEL will not tear it down. Send BYE.

A re-INVITE is a mid-dialog INVITE with a new CSeq. It can carry a new offer. If it changes the remote target in Contact, it is a target refresh and RFC 6141 is the document to read. A 491 Request Pending means the other side has an INVITE outstanding. Wait a short randomized time, as section 14 describes, and retry so the two requests do not collide again.

lessons.title: REFER and Replaces
lessons.summary: REFER asks another UA to send a request, and Replaces names the dialog that request should take over.
objectives: Read Refer-To and the 202 Accepted
Follow progress in NOTIFY sipfrag bodies
Match a Replaces dialog by Call-ID and both tags

illustration.title: Attended transfer
illustration.caption: REFER stays in the original dialog. The INVITE it causes is a new dialog that names the old one.

layers.name: REFER
layers.detail: Refer-To carries the target and the Replaces parameter
The REFER was accepted, not the new call

layers.name: INVITE
layers.detail: Replaces names call-id, to-tag, and from-tag

layers.name: NOTIFY
layers.detail: sipfrag reports how that INVITE is going

paragraphs: RFC 3515 defines REFER. Refer-To is the URI the recipient should request. Referred-By names who asked. The compact forms are r and b. The immediate response is 202 Accepted, which means the request to try was accepted.

The recipient then sends NOTIFY with Event: refer. The body is a sipfrag, a status line such as SIP/2.0 200 OK, showing how the referred request is progressing. 202 is not that result. You have to read the NOTIFY.

RFC 3891 defines Replaces. An attended transfer puts the dialog id into the Refer-To URI as a Replaces parameter, escaped. The UA that receives the resulting INVITE sees a Replaces header with call-id, to-tag, and from-tag.

Those three values are the same dialog identity you already use. If they match a confirmed dialog, the UA accepts the new INVITE and ends the replaced dialog. The early-only parameter limits Replaces to an early dialog. A mismatch is a failed replace, not a new unrelated call you should guess at.

lessons.title: REGISTER and bindings
lessons.summary: REGISTER binds an address-of-record to one or more Contacts, and the registrar is a different role from the proxy.
objectives: Point To at the address-of-record and Contact at the binding
Refresh with the same Call-ID and a higher CSeq
Handle 423 by raising the expiry to Min-Expires

illustration.title: Binding operations
illustration.caption: The 200 OK lists the bindings the registrar is holding after the request.
rows: Expires header or the expires parameter
No other Contact on that request

sections.h: The registrar writes, the proxy reads
paragraphs: Section 10 makes REGISTER the way a UA publishes a Contact for an address-of-record. The To URI is that address-of-record. The Contact URI is the binding. A proxy later consults the location service when an INVITE arrives for the address-of-record.

The registrar and the proxy are different roles. One product often runs both, and the trace still shows REGISTER going to the registrar function and INVITE going to the proxy function. REGISTER does not create a dialog you can BYE. You refresh it with another REGISTER.

Use one Call-ID for the binding and increase CSeq on each REGISTER. The 200 OK returns the current bindings. A 401 carries WWW-Authenticate, and the retry carries Authorization. That challenge is section 22, the same digest model as other UAS challenges, not a 407.

If the requested expiry is shorter than the registrar allows, the response is 423 Interval Too Brief and it includes Min-Expires. Retry with an expiry at least that large. A q parameter on Contact is a preference from 0 to 1, and a larger q is preferred when a proxy forks.

lessons.title: Locating a server with RFC 3263
lessons.summary: RFC 3263 turns a SIP domain into a transport, a port, and an address with NAPTR, SRV, and A or AAAA.
objectives: Order NAPTR, then SRV, then A or AAAA
Name the SIP+D2U, SIP+D2T, and SIPS+D2T services
Skip the name lookup when the Request-URI is already an IP address

illustration.title: Lookup order
illustration.caption: An explicit transport or port skips the records that are no longer needed. A numeric IP skips the name.

sections.h: The domain is not the socket
paragraphs: When the Request-URI host is a domain and the URI does not already dictate transport and port, RFC 3263 starts with NAPTR. The services you will see are SIP+D2U for UDP, SIP+D2T for TCP, and SIPS+D2T for TLS. The NAPTR result names the SRV name to query.

SRV returns a host name and a port. A or AAAA turns that host into an address. The client then writes Via with the transport it selected and sends the SIP request. The DNS messages are not SIP messages. They happen before the first arrow on this ladder.

A numeric IP address in the Request-URI does not need NAPTR or SRV. An explicit port skips the SRV lookup and goes to A or AAAA. An explicit transport parameter selects the NAPTR service instead of leaving the choice open.

Hard-coding 198.51.100.30 will place the next request on that address and will not notice when the SRV target moves. Keep the domain in the Request-URI when you want RFC 3263 to run, and keep the documentation ranges of RFC 5737 out of production.

lessons.title: Loose routing and Max-Forwards
lessons.summary: With lr, the Request-URI stays the remote target, each hop pops its own Route, and Max-Forwards of 0 yields 483.
objectives: Pop a top Route that names this hop
Leave the Request-URI in place when lr is present
Return 483 when Max-Forwards arrives as 0

illustration.title: Two counters on a forwarded request
illustration.caption: Route is the path. Max-Forwards is the budget. They are not substitutes.

paragraphs: A loose router looks at the top Route. If that URI names this hop, the hop removes it. The Request-URI stays the remote target because the Route URI contains lr. The hop then forwards to the next Route, or to the Request-URI when the route set is empty.

Strict routing is the older behavior for a Route URI without lr. Section 16.4 will rewrite the Request-URI in that case. Proxies that follow RFC 3261 put lr on Record-Route so the target the UAC wrote is still the target at the end of the path.

The UAC sets Max-Forwards, and the value SHOULD be 70. A proxy that forwards decrements it by one. If a request arrives with Max-Forwards 0, the proxy does not forward it. For an INVITE that means 483 Too Many Hops.

OPTIONS is the exception that may be answered locally when Max-Forwards is already 0. A loop that should have been a 482 Loop Detected is a different check, based on Via. Do not use 483 as the name for every loop.

lessons.title: Outbound, reg-id, and keepalives
lessons.summary: RFC 5626 binds a UA instance to one or more flows with reg-id and +sip.instance, and keepalives hold those flows open.
objectives: Read reg-id and +sip.instance on Contact
Tell a second flow from a refresh of the first
Name the keepalive used on TCP and on UDP

illustration.title: Same instance, two flows
illustration.caption: The instance URN stays. reg-id changes when the flow changes.
rows: CRLF on TCP, STUN on UDP

paragraphs: RFC 5626 identifies the UA instance with the Contact parameter +sip.instance, whose value is a URN, commonly a UUID URN. reg-id is a positive integer that names one registration flow for that instance.

A second REGISTER with the same instance and a different reg-id is a second flow, which is how a UA keeps a backup path. The same instance and the same reg-id is a refresh of that flow. Supported: outbound is how the UA asks for this behavior. The edge proxy and the registrar use the flow the REGISTER arrived on when they send a later request back.

On TCP and TLS the keepalive is a double CRLF. The peer answers with a single CRLF. On UDP the keepalive is STUN. These messages are defined so a NAT binding and the connection stay up, and so a dead flow can be detected.

A keepalive has no Request-URI, no CSeq, and no dialog. If a trace shows only CRLF on the SIP port, that can be the outbound keepalive rather than a broken INVITE. The SIP registration beside it is what created the flow.

lessons.title: Path and Service-Route
lessons.summary: Path is the inbound vector stored with a binding, and Service-Route is the outbound vector the registrar gives the UA.
objectives: Insert Path on REGISTER the way a proxy inserts Record-Route
Use Service-Route as a preloaded Route for a new request
Keep the two vectors from being swapped

illustration.title: In versus out
illustration.caption: Both headers look like Route URIs. They are learned at registration and they point in opposite directions.

layers.name: Path
layers.detail: Edge inserts it. Registrar stores it with the binding.

layers.name: Inbound INVITE
layers.detail: Registrar puts that Path on the Route toward the UA.

layers.name: Service-Route
layers.detail: Registrar returns it in the 200 OK.

layers.name: Outbound INVITE
layers.detail: UA preloads it as Route.

sections.h: Path is Record-Route for a binding
paragraphs: RFC 3327 defines Path. A proxy between the UA and the registrar inserts a Path URI, with lr, on the REGISTER. The registrar stores that vector with the Contact. The 200 OK echoes Path so the UA can see it.

When a request later arrives for that address-of-record, the registrar or home proxy places the stored Path into Route so the request reaches the UA through the same edge. Path is not the dialog route set. The dialog route set still comes from Record-Route on the INVITE.

RFC 3608 defines Service-Route. The registrar puts it on the 200 OK to REGISTER. The UA saves those URIs and uses them as a preloaded Route on requests that are not yet inside a dialog, such as the first INVITE.

Service-Route does not tell the network how to reach the UA. Path does that. Swapping them sends the outbound call back at the UA or sends the inbound call at the home proxy with no edge. Supported: path is how the UA indicates it understands the inbound vector.

lessons.title: GRUU and a single instance
lessons.summary: A GRUU routes to one UA instance, and the registrar returns it as pub-gruu or temp-gruu on the binding.
objectives: Register with Supported: gruu and +sip.instance
Distinguish a public GRUU from a temporary GRUU

illustration.title: Where the request can land
illustration.caption: The gr parameter marks a GRUU. The instance URN is what the registrar bound.
rows: Hides the AOR and can change

sections.h: Ask for a URI that means this instance
paragraphs: RFC 5627 defines the GRUU. The UA registers with Supported: gruu and a +sip.instance URN on the Contact. The registrar returns pub-gruu and temp-gruu parameters on that Contact in the 200 OK.

A public GRUU is stable enough to hand to another party. It is often the address-of-record plus a gr parameter that carries the instance. A temporary GRUU is minted so the far end cannot use it to learn the address-of-record, and the registrar can change it.

An INVITE to the address-of-record may fork to every Contact. An INVITE to a GRUU is routed to the instance that registered that GRUU. The gr parameter is the marker that this URI is a GRUU rather than an ordinary address-of-record.

The home proxy still uses Path or the registered flow to reach the instance. A GRUU does not mean the Contact IP is globally reachable. It means the logical target is one UA, not the whole set of bindings.

lessons.title: Forking and early dialogs
lessons.summary: A forking proxy creates one client transaction per binding, and each To tag is a separate early dialog.
objectives: Give each branch its own Via branch
Key early dialogs on the remote tag
Forward every 2xx and cancel other branches on a 6xx

illustration.title: One INVITE, two early dialogs
illustration.caption: Call-ID and the From tag match. The To tags do not. That is two dialogs.

sections.h: One server transaction, many client transactions
paragraphs: A stateful proxy that forks sends a separate client transaction to each target. Each gets its own Via branch. The Call-ID, From tag, and CSeq number stay the ones from the caller. 100 Trying from a downstream branch is not forwarded. The proxy already generated 100 on the upstream hop if it needed to.

A provisional response with a To tag creates an early dialog for that branch. Two 180 responses with different To tags are two early dialogs, even though the Call-ID matches. The UAC has to keep both.

sections.h: What a final response does to the other branches
paragraphs: A 2xx is forwarded immediately, and another 2xx on a different branch is also forwarded. The UAC ACKs each 2xx. The application can BYE the dialog it will not keep. A proxy does not treat the first 200 OK as permission to invent a CANCEL for the others.

A 6xx is different. The proxy should cancel the client transactions that are still pending and it must not open new branches. It does not forward the 6xx until that cancel step has run, so the caller does not see a 6xx followed by a 2xx. Other 4xx and 5xx responses wait so the proxy can choose the best one after the branches settle.
